title: THE PATTERN BEHIND LOSING YOUR PASSION FOR GOD: You Rarely Wake Up One Morning and Stop Loving Jesus—It Usually Dies One Small Compromise at a Time
paragraphs:
THE PATTERN BEHIND LOSING YOUR PASSION FOR GOD: You Rarely Wake Up One Morning and Stop Loving Jesus—It Usually Dies One Small Compromise at a Time
You still believe. You still know the verses. You may even still go to church. But somewhere between the person who once couldn't get enough of God and the person staring back at you today… something went cold. And Jesus warned us this could happen.
There was a time when you didn't have to force yourself to pray.
There was a time when opening your Bible didn't feel like another responsibility waiting to be completed.
One worship song could bring tears to your eyes.
One reminder of the cross could make everything else in your life suddenly seem small.
You talked to Jesus in the car.
You whispered His name before falling asleep.
You thought about Him when nobody was watching.
You wanted your friends to know Him.
You hated the thought of disappointing Him—not because you were terrified He would stop loving you, but because you were beginning to understand just how much He had loved you first.
There may have been no announcement.
No moment when you stood before God and said, "I don't want You anymore."
Maybe you never rejected Jesus at all.
Things that once bothered your conscience slowly became easier to tolerate.
at least you kept telling yourself you did.
But somehow you could spend two hours consuming entertainment and feel irritated after ten minutes alone with Him.
Talk for an hour about something that excited you when exhausted.
But when it came time to pray?
And perhaps the most dangerous part was that your Christian life continued functioning well enough that almost nobody noticed.
“Because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold.” — Matthew 24:12
“διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνομίαν, ψυγήσεται ἡ ἀγάπη τῶν πολλῶν.”
Jesus was describing a world in which increasing ἀνομία—anomia, lawlessness—would be accompanied by the chilling of love.
A heart that once burned can cool.
And perhaps that explains something you have been unable to put into words.
You didn't necessarily stop believing in God.
And spiritual coldness usually has a pattern.
It begins when something else starts receiving what once belonged to God.
At first, the replacement doesn't have to look evil.
Sometimes what steals your passion for God isn't obvious wickedness.
Even good things become dangerous when they begin occupying the throne reserved for the Giver.
And slowly, almost invisibly, your soul becomes accustomed to living on crumbs while sitting feet away from the Bread of Life.
You tell yourself you're just busy.
And eventually you can remember the person you used to be with God more clearly than you recognize the person you've become.
But it should not make us despair.
Because Scripture shows us that God has confronted this pattern before.
Through Jeremiah, God spoke to a people who had wandered:
“I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness…”
The Hebrew contains this beautiful expression:
the love associated with your betrothal, your bridal love.
God remembered when His people followed Him into the wilderness.
They exchanged the glory of God for substitutes that could never satisfy them.
And that is still the anatomy of spiritual drift.
We rarely decide, “Today I will destroy my relationship with God.”
And every trade seems too small to matter.
Until one day you realize you traded a fire for ashes.
Maybe you're reading this and thinking:
I remember praying because I couldn't imagine not praying.
I remember worshipping when nobody was watching.
And because you feel numb, perhaps you've concluded that God must be far away.
But before you accuse God of moving, ask yourself a painful question:
There is a moment in Revelation 2 that every serious Christian should wrestle with.
Jesus speaks to the church in Ephesus.
These weren't people who had abandoned Christian activity.
From the outside, this could look like a strong church.
“But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.”
“Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first.”
Jesus doesn't tell them to manufacture goosebumps.
He doesn't tell them to wait for a worship song powerful enough to make them emotional again.
He calls them to remember where they have fallen from, repent, and return to faithful action.
Because maybe you've been waiting to feel passionate before you start pursuing God again.
What if you open the Bible while your emotions are still cold?
What if you kneel while prayer still feels difficult?
What if you confess the sin before you feel sufficiently sorry?
What if you delete what keeps pulling you back?
What if you return to church?
What if you tell another believer the truth about what has been happening inside you?
What if instead of waiting for the fire…
you start bringing God the wood?
Because passion for God isn't sustained by chasing spiritual emotion.
It grows from seeing Christ clearly, abiding in Him, believing His Gospel, obeying His Word, walking by His Spirit, and continually returning to the astonishing reality of what Jesus has done.
Not the decorative cross around someone's neck.
Not the polished cross hanging inside a sanctuary.
The innocent One dying for the guilty.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because humanity was impressive.
He went because humanity was lost.
Your salvation was never the story of a decent person becoming slightly better.
The Gospel is far more scandalous than that.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we failed to live, gave Himself for sinners, died, was buried, and rose victorious.
Grace is not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves how terribly sin matters.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
That is why repentance isn't punishment.
And maybe that's what you need right now.
Maybe your prayer life has collapsed.
Maybe pornography has quietly hollowed out your spiritual appetite.
Maybe bitterness has been sitting in your chest so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe you've been sleeping with someone you know you shouldn't.
Maybe money owns more of your heart than Jesus does.
Maybe nobody knows what you're doing behind closed doors.
Maybe you're not living in obvious scandal at all.
Maybe you're simply spiritually exhausted and distracted and you've forgotten how to sit quietly in the presence of God.
But don't confuse “come home” with “God doesn't care how you live.”
Jesus did not die merely to make us comfortable while we remain enslaved to what destroys us.
The Christ who receives sinners calls sinners to follow Him.
And this is where the enemy has deceived many people.
He tells the rebellious person, “God doesn't care.”
Then when the rebellious person finally wakes up, he changes the message:
And you are not saved by earning God's affection.
Jesus is not waiting for you to become impressive enough to approach Him.
The son rehearsed his confession and headed home.
But while he was still far away, his father saw him.
Then one of the most breathtaking pictures of grace in Scripture unfolds.
The father was moved with compassion.
The Greek text of Luke 15:20 intensifies the scene with κατεφίλησεν—katephilēsen—he kissed him affectionately.
The son came home carrying the smell of his rebellion.
The father ran toward him anyway.
And if you have wandered from God, please understand this:
Satan wants you staring at the pigpen until you forget there is a Father to run home to.
Stop negotiating with the thing that's killing your love for Christ.
Stop calling bondage “just something I'm struggling with” if you've secretly decided to protect it forever.
Not because sin is insignificant, but because Christ is a greater Savior than you imagined.
David knew what it meant for sin to devastate the inner life.
After the horror of his sin was exposed, Psalm 51 records one of Scripture's most desperate prayers of repentance.
And listen to what David asks:
“Restore to me the joy of Your salvation.”
David did not ask God to help him fake enthusiasm.
And notice whose salvation it is.
That means if your heart has grown cold, the answer isn't pretending you're still on fire.
It's admitting you're cold enough to need God to rekindle what you cannot manufacture.
Maybe your most honest prayer tonight isn't impressive.
“Jesus, I don't even know when I changed.”
“Lord, I have wanted Your gifts more than You.”
“I don't feel what I used to feel, but I want to want You again.”
God is not intimidated by an honest prayer.
Ask Him to expose what has been cooling your love.
Then be willing to surrender it.
Because we cannot repeatedly feed what numbs us and then wonder why we're spiritually numb.
We cannot continually rehearse bitterness and wonder why worship feels empty.
We cannot feast on lust all week and wonder why holiness feels tasteless.
We cannot give every spare second to noise and wonder why we cannot hear the whisper of Scripture in our minds.
We cannot treat Jesus like an emergency contact and expect intimacy to flourish.
A relationship starved of attention will feel distant.
The Christian life isn't primarily about having one dramatic encounter with Jesus twenty years ago.
It's about continuing with Him today.
And when you understand what God is doing.
Faithfulness is not proved only by how loudly you worship when you feel God.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like opening Scripture with tears in your eyes and saying:
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something else.
Your loss of emotional intensity does not automatically mean you've abandoned God.
We pass through seasons where emotions change.
Christian maturity should not be measured solely by whether every prayer gives you chills.
There is a difference between emotional dryness and deliberate spiritual drift.
Sometimes mature love feels less like fireworks and more like staying.
“Do I feel what I used to feel?”
“Am I obeying what He has shown me?”
“Am I confessing sin rather than protecting it?”
And when the answer exposes something painful…
That's where grace begins doing surgery.
You don't need to impress Jesus.
That is the pattern behind losing passion for God.
And eventually the heart grows cold.
And then tell someone else if you need accountability.
And if God has been restoring you already, tell us what He has done. Your testimony may become the exact thing another wounded believer needs to read tonight.
Somebody else may see it and realize they're not the only one fighting.
Somebody may finally confess what they've been hiding because you were brave enough to go first.
This is what Christian community should look like—not a museum full of people pretending they never struggled, but redeemed sinners pointing one another toward Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves you're a better Christian. It doesn't.
But if this message is biblically faithful and you believe someone in your circle needs to return to Jesus, sharing it can be one simple act of witness.
Think about the person who has stopped going to church.
The friend whose faith has quietly gone cold.
The mother spiritually exhausted from holding everybody together.
The Christian who looks perfectly fine online but cries when nobody is looking.
Send it privately if publicly tagging them would embarrass them.
Even invite the person who doesn't believe yet.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people, creating biblical resources, strengthening believers, and putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it.
If you want to glorify God through your resources, Scripture gives us a far bigger vision than merely clicking a button: steward what He has entrusted to you for His purposes.
And there is something else we want you to know.
Because we don't simply want you inspired for five minutes.
And increasingly transformed into the likeness of Jesus Christ.
The One who was crucified for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still receives repentant people.
The One who knows exactly how cold your heart has become and is not shocked by what He finds.
The One who can restore the joy you've lost.
Maybe that's why you kept reading.
Maybe beneath all the distractions, compromises, disappointment, exhaustion, shame, and spiritual numbness…
there is still a tiny ache.
The story does not have to end with the fire going out.
Peter failed spectacularly and Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted and Jesus met him.
The prodigal wandered and came home.
David fell into devastating sin and cried out for a clean heart.
The cross itself looked like the darkest scandal imaginable until resurrection morning revealed that God was writing redemption through what looked like defeat.
And maybe your chapter right now is ugly.
Maybe there are paragraphs you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are pages you are ashamed anybody could ever read.
But the Gospel has never been about pretending the scandal didn't happen.
It is about what Jesus does with sinners who surrender their stories to Him.
Let Him restore what sin damaged.
Let Him expose what distraction buried.
Let Him become precious to you again.
If this pierced you, comment before you leave.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy isn't discovering that your heart has grown cold.
Perhaps the greater tragedy would be discovering it…
and choosing to remain where you are.
You may remember the moment your fire started dying—but by the grace of Jesus Christ, that does not have to be the final sentence of your story.
